stimulus: City transit planner: Ridership on the Elm Street bus line rose eleven percent in the six months after we widened the sidewalks along its route. Some colleagues credit the systemwide fare discount introduced around the same time. But that discount applied to every line in the network, while no other line gained riders at anything near that rate. The sidewalk project made walking to Elm Street stops easier, and that improved access is what drove the gain.
question_stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the planner's argument?
choice_a: After the sidewalks were widened, several regular Elm Street riders reported that they would have begun riding the line even without the improvements.
choice_b: Boarding records show that nearly all of the additional Elm Street trips began at stops located within the blocks where sidewalks were widened, and few began elsewhere on the line.
choice_c: Citywide surveys show that residents consider convenient access among the most important factors in choosing how to commute.
choice_d: The eleven percent increase on Elm Street began in the very month that the sidewalk project was completed.
choice_e: The Elm Street line now carries more riders than the Oak Avenue line, which serves a similar number of households.
prediction_text: Find new evidence tying the ridership gain specifically to easier walking access, not to timing or general preferences.
trap_c: supports a broader claim than the concluded link (survivor)
trap_d: restates the timing correlation as support
trap_e: comparison that never touches the mechanism
explanation_a: Riders saying they would have come anyway cuts against improved access as the driver; it weakens rather than strengthens.
explanation_b: Correct. Locating the new trips at the widened-sidewalk stops directly confirms the access mechanism the planner proposes.
explanation_c: A general preference for access citywide does not connect this line's specific gain to these sidewalks.
explanation_d: The argument already rests on this timing; repeating the correlation adds no support for the causal claim.
explanation_e: How Elm Street compares with another line says nothing about why Elm Street's own ridership rose.
